story.text:
Thank you, Reed. Hello everybody. My name is Zach, and I'm going to take you through *magic*, a history.

I first learned of magic when I was 7 years old and my mom came home from Blockbuster with the original **Final Fantasy** game. This was my original party: a fighter, a thief, a white mage, and a black mage. I remember thinking: *If I could make magic real, I could help all my friends.* That became a lifelong obsession.

In 2000 I came to **Reed College**, which brought me to Portland. My number at the time was **503-771-1112**, the Reed switchboard. Back then no one had cell phones, so if you needed a call, it went through the switchboard, then to your dorm, and then someone would holler for you. It’s important for this digital-identity story, because if you go to any store in Portland with a loyalty program, you can enter that number—I've been using it for 20 years—and Kroger has no idea who I am.

For various reasons I had to leave Reed, came back in 2010, ran out of money again, dropped out again. I've dropped out of college three times: twice from Reed, once from somewhere else. I like to tell people I'm the *second* most famous Reed dropout—trying to become the first.

After dropping out the second time, I got a job at **Globe Sherpa**, makers of the original TriMet tickets app. I was employee #1 and the mobile guy. I built the app that predates the current Hop Fastpass app. In 2015 we were acquired by Daimler. I was put on R&D—this was the moment when all car companies were panicking about autonomous vehicles and Tesla; scooters were coming out; and they were hedging bets with “mobility companies.”

Our mandate: **figure out how to turn today’s bus riders into tomorrow’s Mercedes drivers**. I said: *You’re going to need a lot of scholarships.*

When Reed walked in today he asked, “This isn’t about crypto, is it?” Don’t worry—it’s *not* about crypto.

But as we all know, crypto was invented in the 1600s by the **Yap Islanders** who used giant stone disks as currency. The stones were too heavy to move, so they used a **distributed ledger**—everyone kept track of who owned which rock.
In 2008 the technology was rediscovered by… whoever this is.

There’s one line in the Bitcoin abstract: **“Digital signatures provide part of the solution.”**
I thought: *What the hell is a digital signature?* That got me deeply intrigued.

Then I had an epiphany. My favorite band, **Jawbreaker**, was playing for the first time in 20 years. They had broken up before I was old enough to go to shows. They were playing in Chicago, where I’m from. I had to go. In the Denver airport, thinking about crypto and digital signatures, I had this vision:

If this is the blockchain—many computers doing the *same* thing—what if instead they did **different** things? Rotate the picture: a bunch of computers linked together doing useful things in a chain. Not a single chain—**multiple chains**. I didn’t know what it was yet, but it seemed cool.

It felt like this: in the 5th century BCE Euclid wrote down geometry based on five postulates. Four are straightforward. The fifth is long and weird. It took humanity 2,000 years to realize that if you *remove* the fifth, you get **two other kinds of geometry**.

Back to my picture: in blockchain all the nodes must agree on identity. But what if you had computers *outside* the chain whose job was to tell you **who the person is**, and inside the chain everyone just *trusts* those identity computers?

We didn’t know what these identity-computers were. This was 2017. At Globe Sherpa we were working with transit agencies. Transit touches every part of a city. Our big client was **Ventra** in Chicago. They wanted systems that could interact with all the vendors along their routes. You *can't*, because every shop has its own identity system.

Then a call for papers came from ACM for a Smart Cities conference in Portland in 2018. A colleague and I wrote **“Digital Identity for Smart Cities.”**
TL;DR: *It should never be my responsibility to tell you who I am.* If you're a computer system and want to know who I am, **you should tell me who I am in your system**, and I’ll carry that around—like government papers, but digital.

Everybody tries to get your email/password so they can market to you. I won’t belabor digital identity and privacy with this crowd. Just give me a **UUID** and let me go.

I told this idea to a friend at **Galois** (the cybersecurity company). He said it was good. We thought the missing piece preventing global adoption was a missing **cross-language cryptographic standard**.

He went off and founded a B2B company with the idea; I started a B2C company: **Planet 9**—named after the hypothetical planet past Neptune (formerly “Planet X,” downgraded after Pluto was demoted).

Planet 9’s goal was to **remonetize the internet**:
“**Change the world by giving everybody five bucks.**”

If you need $40B to give everyone $5, it has to come from somewhere, so we targeted **advertising**—the system that exists only to extract data and rent-seek.

I wrote lots of code. The company wasn’t the right thing. Then the pandemic came.
I had my son, Finn, in 2022. I realized time was up: I’d open-source everything.

I posted on Reddit, got invited to an open-source Discord run by “WickedRose,” a brilliant hobbyist who writes pro-level Bash on a computer nailed under his TV. The community grew from 250 to 2,500 people in two years, worldwide, with hundreds of projects. It gave me deep insight into global priorities and problems.

Meanwhile I was also in the **Dorkbot** Discord. At my day job (Homes.com / Apartments.com) I was prepping a talk on Agile and saw **Ward Cunningham’s** name on the Agile Manifesto. I recognized him from Dorkbot PDX. I pinged him in January. We got to talking: he had **Federated Wiki**; I was building digital identity and a backend-as-a-service system. I needed federation. We met for drinks and clicked.

That motivated me to start shipping. Two weeks later I released the “magic and teleportation” video. That led to a whole year of work.

**Advancement** is the consumer-facing part of this “digital identity magic stuff.” The picture shows the groups using it this past year. They don’t share a single theme because identity touches everything:

* **Mirllo** — a Bandcamp alternative
* **Swedom** — a nonprofit giving center in McMinnville
* **Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy** — Robbie Stamp (Douglas Adams’s longtime friend and CEO) is using it to build federated community guides worldwide. Hitchhikers shouldn’t need to announce who they “really are.”

All these groups are nonprofits—and nonprofits often don’t make money. So we’re building **alternatives to the top 35 ecommerce platforms charging >9% fees**. With standard identity, we can build reusable systems communities can deploy.

One such community: **The Fledge** in Lansing, serving 100,000 people per year with entrepreneurship and adult education. The first target: **Link aggregators** (Linktree etc.).
Those companies just raised prices from $9/mo to $15/mo—a 66% increase—for essentially four links on a PNG.

So I built **Linkity Link** and handed it to The Fledge. Jerry, who runs it, said, “They just canceled my subscription two days ago.” He can now push Linkity Link to his community—sell 5,000 of them for $20, and keep the money.

Next is **Bisbuzz**, digital business cards.
Then **Leiddki**, a Trello knockoff named for Katie Ledecky. I name projects after inspiring women—it’s an open namespace.

Which brings us back to **magic**.

Magic works because if you’ve ever built a large backend, you know microservices were cool for a minute—now everyone hates them—because **auth** was always the problem. It slowed everything down.

But with **Magic**, using **digital signatures flowing through you**, you can send authorized requests through multiple machines. You can chain them. That’s a **spell**. There’s a whole namespace for spells. You can build them *without writing code*. Once you have a spell-authorizing system, you can create spells that do interesting things—including paid work.

The original patent I wrote (never filed) called Magic:

**Multi-device Asynchronous Generic Input Output Consensus.**
Lawyers removed “magic”—patent office doesn’t like people calling things magic.

But I’ve realized that’s the wrong backronym. The real one is:

**Multi-party Assistive Generosity In a Community.**

That’s my Magic today.

---

## **Demo**

(On the right) a BLE bridge.
(On the left) a website running from a server.
Hardware: an Unexpected Maker Pro S3 ESP32 board.

(Disclaimer: the signatures aren’t in the demo version—I removed them because I was having trouble—but it normally works.)

Start the bridge, it listens for messages. The device connects. Press the capacitive pin. The message goes from device → bridge → server → browser and back. You can chain arbitrary machines.

Example: **DoorDash**. Today: user → DoorDash → restaurant → driver.
Magic: **restaurant ↔ driver ↔ customer**, no platform in the middle. A straight line instead of a triangle.

There’s someone building a… “ride-sharing application evocative of Lyft” using this system.

A colleague from the Smart Cities paper is now Director of Special Projects at TriMet—we’ve talked about using this system for deliveries and day-to-day service work.

---

# **Q&A (lightly cleaned)**

**Q:** How do you prevent a bad actor from inserting their own Bluetooth device?
**A:** Follow the “Portland method of security”: don’t put things of value on the network. Transactions aren’t *giving*, they’re *trading*. A bad actor can only harm the system if value passes through them. Messages are **digitally signed**, so gateways are known to the resolver. Bad actors can be removed by implementation-level policy (e.g., reputation, banning).

**Q:** I don’t hear anything in the protocol about reputation.
**A:** Correct. The protocol is minimal. Reputation systems can be layered on top.

**Q:** Without a trusted authority, crowd-sourcing trust becomes chaos. How do you avoid that?
**A:** Ward Cunningham’s answer: *Why do you trust the authority?*
The protocol allows communities to build trust mechanisms. Implementations can stay small—where people actually know one another.

**Q:** Is there end-to-end encryption?
**A:** Not required. Only digital signatures matter for authenticity. You *can* use encrypted transports like HTTPS. BLE in the demo wasn’t encrypted, but could be.

**Q:** How do *you* get paid?
**A:** I don’t. I’ve been doing this for free for ten years. I have sold 12 books at $5 each—so $60 total!
Long-term plan: create a **royalty-based digital value exchange for open-source software**, like royalties for music/books/movies.

**Q:** How do *you* get paid?
**A:** I don’t. I’ve been doing this for free for ten years. I have sold 12 books at $5 each—so $60 total!
Long-term plan: create a **royalty-based digital value exchange for open-source software**, like royalties for music/books/movies.
